newsitem.title: GERMANY: New Leica shares surge in bourse debut.
newsitem.headline: New Leica shares surge in bourse debut.

text.p: Newly issued shares in Germany's prestige camera maker Leica Camera Gruppe soared nearly 13 percent above their issue price in their Frankfurt bourse debut on Thursday.

The shares whose price at issue was set last week at 47 marks ($31.12) -- the top end of their bookbuilding range -- surged as high as 53.50 marks in an almost static broader market before closing the floor session at 53 marks, up six marks.

The 80-year old German company, a unit of Switzerland's Leica Group, has sold off 3.1 million shares with total nominal value of 15.58 million marks, or five marks each, in an initial issue which it said was over-subscribed.
A total of 201,232 Leica shares changed hands during the first day's trade, which was neatly timed to coincide with the German camera trade fair Photokina, running this week in the city of Cologne.

Leica plans to use its new capital to finance new technologies and a push into high growth markets like Asia and has said in the past it may also issue a further greenshoe package of 2.25 million marks nominal value in shares.
The company was unavailable for comment on its future plans on Thursday. Its share offer was managed by Union Bank of Switzerland and Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank.
The Leica shares carry full dividend rights to the current business year ending March 31 1997.
Last year, Leica raised its sales by 4.7 percent to 240 million marks and its operating earnings by 15.3 percent to 16.5 million and said it hoped to at least match those levels in the current year.

The company, best known for its respected M6 rangefinder camera and M6 lens system, is focusing more on high-margin products such as cameras, projectors and specialist optical equipment as well as cutting costs in order to boost its earnings.

Announcing group results in July and heralding the share issue, management board chairman Klaus-Dieter Hofmann also said Leica had set its sights on the Far East, where its sales rose 44 percent to 18.7 percent of all turnover last year.

While Germany remains Leica's core market and accounted for 42.2 percent of group sales last year, Leica estimates that the Japanese use five rolls of film each a year, compared with just 2.2 rolls for the average German snapper.
